topic: What if all the oxygen in Earth's air vanished for five seconds?
scientific_scope_note: Only the oxygen gas in the air disappears for five seconds; oxygen bound in water, rock, ozone and living tissue stays. The one-fifth pressure drop and 2 km altitude equivalence are derived approximations; ear discomfort, aircraft behaviour and power-grid disruption are illustrative possibilities, not forecasts.

narration.caption_alignment: whisper-small.en word timestamps on the synthesized audio (local)
script: What if all the oxygen in the air vanished, for just five seconds?
Oxygen makes up about a fifth of the air. Take it away, and the whole atmosphere instantly thins.
Air pressure would plunge by about a fifth. Sea level would suddenly feel like a mountain, two kilometers high.
Your ears would pop, hard. But you wouldn't suffocate. Your blood already carries enough oxygen to ride out those seconds.
Fire is another story. Every flame that feeds on air would go out at once.
Jet engines would flame out. Airliners would sag in the thinner air, gliding until those engines could relight.
Birds would dip mid-flight. But underwater, fish would hardly notice. The oxygen dissolved in the sea stays put.
Then the oxygen rushes back. Hot embers flare to life again. But power plants that lost their flames could stay dark for hours.
Five seconds without oxygen wouldn't end the world. It would show us how much of it still runs on fire.

youtube_shorts.title: What If Earth's Air Lost Its Oxygen for 5 Seconds?
youtube_shorts.description:
What would really happen if all the oxygen in the air vanished for five seconds, then came back? This 3D thought experiment follows the missing oxygen from a candle flame to orbit and home again.

• Oxygen is about a fifth of the air, so air pressure would drop by about a fifth. Sea level would feel like roughly 2 km of altitude.
• Your ears would pop, but you wouldn't suffocate: your blood already carries enough oxygen for a few seconds.
• Every flame that feeds on air would go out. Jet engines would flame out and airliners would sag in the thinner air.
• Fish would hardly notice, because the oxygen dissolved in the sea stays put.
• When the oxygen returns, hot embers can flare back to life, but power plants that lost their flames could stay dark for hours.

Scope: only the oxygen gas in the air is removed. Aircraft and blackout outcomes are labelled illustrative in the film; they are possibilities, not predictions.

Sources: NASA Earth Fact Sheet, NOAA JetStream (air pressure), USGS Water Science School (dissolved oxygen), NASA Glenn (lift equation). Earth imagery: NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble. Narration, music and sound are synthesized.
